l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 7
s: In Judges 7, Gideon (also called Jerubbaal) and the Israelite army camp at the spring of Harod opposite the Midianite camp in the valley. The LORD says the army is too large, so Gideon sends home twenty-two thousand fearful men, and a test at the water reduces the remaining ten thousand to three hundred who lapped. Encouraged by a Midianite's dream of a barley cake overturning a tent and its interpretation as Gideon's sword, Gideon divides the three hundred into three companies armed with trumpets, empty pitchers, and torches. At night they blow trumpets, break the pitchers, and shout, and the LORD sets the Midianites' swords against one another so the army flees. Men from Naphtali, Asher, Manasseh, and Ephraim pursue, and the Ephraimites capture and kill the princes Oreb and Zeeb and bring their heads to Gideon beyond the Jordan.

l: Gideon, The Book of Judges, Chapter 7
s: Gideon, also called Jerubbaal, camps at the spring of Harod, reduces his army at the LORD's direction, and goes down to the Midianite camp with Purah his servant. After hearing the dream and its interpretation he worships, divides the three hundred men into three companies, and leads the trumpet-and-pitcher attack. He then summons the men of Ephraim to take the waters to the Jordan and receives the heads of Oreb and Zeeb.

l: LORD, The Book of Judges, Chapter 7
s: The LORD tells Gideon the army is too large so that Israel cannot brag that its own hand saved it, and directs the reduction by proclamation and by the test at the water. He promises to save Israel by the three hundred, assures Gideon that the Midianite camp is delivered into his hand, and sets every Midianite's sword against his fellow during the attack.

l: Israel, The Book of Judges, Chapter 7
s: Israel is the people for whom the LORD gives victory over Midian, and the LORD wants to prevent it from claiming the victory as its own. Men of Israel from Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh gather and pursue Midian after the army flees.

l: Midian, The Book of Judges, Chapter 7
s: The Midianites, with the Amalekites and the children of the east, lie in the valley like locusts, with camels as countless as sand. Terrified by the trumpets, shouts, and torches, they flee, and the LORD sets their swords against one another. They are pursued as far as Beth Shittah, Abel Meholah, and the Jordan, and their princes Oreb and Zeeb are killed.

l: three hundred men (Gideon's chosen men), The Book of Judges, Chapter 7
s: The three hundred are the men who lapped water with their hands to their mouths, and the LORD says he will save Israel by them. Gideon divides them into three companies, each man carrying a trumpet and a pitcher with a torch inside, and they stand around the Midianite camp and carry out the night attack.

l: people (Israelite fighters with Gideon), The Book of Judges, Chapter 7
s: Of the people with Gideon, twenty-two thousand return home after the proclamation for the fearful, leaving ten thousand. The test at the water reduces these to three hundred, and the rest are sent to their tents after taking food and their trumpets.

l: Ephraim, The Book of Judges, Chapter 7
s: Gideon sends messengers throughout the hill country of Ephraim, calling the men to come down against Midian and take the waters as far as Beth Barah and the Jordan. All the men of Ephraim gather and do so, and they take and kill the Midianite princes Oreb and Zeeb.

l: Oreb, The Book of Judges, Chapter 7
s: Oreb is one of the two princes of Midian taken by the Ephraimites. He is killed at Oreb's rock, and his head is brought to Gideon beyond the Jordan.

l: Zeeb, The Book of Judges, Chapter 7
s: Zeeb is one of the two princes of Midian taken by the Ephraimites. He is killed at Zeeb's wine press, and his head is brought to Gideon beyond the Jordan.

l: dream of the barley cake, The Book of Judges, Chapter 7
s: A Midianite tells his fellow that he dreamed a cake of barley bread tumbled into the camp and struck a tent so that it lay flat. His fellow interprets it as the sword of Gideon, with God delivering Midian and its army into his hand. Gideon overhears this, worships, and returns to rouse Israel.

l: test at the water, The Book of Judges, Chapter 7
s: At the LORD's direction Gideon brings the ten thousand down to the water, where those who lap with the tongue like a dog, putting a hand to the mouth, are set apart from those who bow on their knees to drink. Three hundred lap, and the LORD chooses them to save Israel while the rest are sent home.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 8
s: Gideon calms the men of Ephraim, who rebuke him for not calling them, by praising their capture of the Midianite princes Oreb and Zeeb. He then pursues the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna with his three hundred men, but the men of Succoth and Penuel refuse them bread. Gideon defeats the remaining Midianite army, captures the two kings, punishes Succoth with thorns and briers and destroys the tower of Penuel while killing its men, and kills Zebah and Zalmunna because they had killed his brothers at Tabor. The men of Israel offer to make Gideon ruler, which he refuses, but he collects gold earrings and makes an ephod that becomes a snare as Israel plays the prostitute with it. After forty years of rest Gideon dies, and Israel turns to the Baals and fails to show kindness to Gideon's house.

l: Gideon, The Book of Judges, Chapter 8
s: Gideon placates the men of Ephraim, pursues Zebah and Zalmunna with three hundred faint men, punishes Succoth and Penuel for refusing bread, and kills the two kings in revenge for his brothers killed at Tabor. He refuses to rule Israel, saying the LORD shall rule, but makes an ephod from collected gold that becomes a snare to him and his house. He has seventy sons by many wives and a son Abimelech by a concubine in Shechem, and dies in a good old age, buried in Ophrah.

l: Midian, The Book of Judges, Chapter 8
s: Midian is subdued before the children of Israel and lifts up its head no more. Its remaining army of about fifteen thousand men, left after one hundred twenty thousand fell, is struck by Gideon while feeling secure, and its two kings are captured and killed.

l: LORD, The Book of Judges, Chapter 8
s: God is credited by Gideon's words with delivering the Midianite princes Oreb and Zeeb into Ephraim's hand, and Gideon says the LORD will deliver Zebah and Zalmunna to him. Gideon declares that the LORD shall rule over Israel. After Gideon's death, Israel does not remember the LORD their God, who had delivered them from all their enemies.

l: Succoth, The Book of Judges, Chapter 8
s: The princes of Succoth refuse Gideon's request for bread for his faint men, mocking whether Zebah and Zalmunna are already in his hand. After the capture, Gideon learns from a young man the names of its princes and elders, seventy-seven men, and takes the elders and teaches the men of Succoth with thorns and briers.

l: Zebah, The Book of Judges, Chapter 8
s: Zebah, a king of Midian, is in Karkor with an army when Gideon strikes it; he flees, is captured, and is questioned about the men killed at Tabor. Gideon kills him along with Zalmunna after learning those men were his brothers.

l: Zalmunna, The Book of Judges, Chapter 8
s: Zalmunna, a king of Midian, is in Karkor with Zebah and flees but is captured by Gideon. He and Zebah say that as the man is, so is his strength, and Gideon kills them and takes the crescents from their camels' necks.

l: Penuel, The Book of Judges, Chapter 8
s: The men of Penuel answer Gideon's request for bread as Succoth did, and Gideon vows to break down their tower when he returns in peace. He later breaks down the tower of Penuel and kills the men of the city.

l: Israel, The Book of Judges, Chapter 8
s: The men of Israel ask Gideon to rule over them, with his son and grandson, because he saved them from Midian. They willingly give their plunder's golden earrings, then play the prostitute with the ephod, and after Gideon dies they turn to the Baals, forget the LORD, and show no kindness to Gideon's house.

l: ephod, The Book of Judges, Chapter 8
s: Gideon makes the ephod from the gold earrings collected, which weighed one thousand seven hundred shekels, and puts it in Ophrah, his city. All Israel plays the prostitute with it there, and it becomes a snare to Gideon and his house.

l: Baals, The Book of Judges, Chapter 8
s: After Gideon's death, the children of Israel turn again and play the prostitute following the Baals. They make Baal Berith their god.

l: battle with Midian, The Book of Judges, Chapter 8
s: The Ephraimites complain they were not called to the fight, and Gideon soothes them by citing their capture of Oreb and Zeeb. Gideon's three hundred men pursue and strike the Midianite army of about fifteen thousand at Karkor, confuse it, and capture Zebah and Zalmunna. The victory leaves Midian subdued and the land at rest for forty years.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 9
s: Abimelech, son of Jerubbaal, persuades the men of Shechem to back him, hires reckless men with silver from the house of Baal Berith, kills his seventy brothers at Ophrah on one stone, and is made king; only Jotham survives by hiding. Jotham tells the parable of the trees from Mount Gerizim and curses Abimelech and Shechem with mutual fire, then flees to Beer. After three years God sends an evil spirit between them, and Shechem turns on Abimelech, backing Gaal the son of Ebed, who is defeated through the warning of Zebul and driven out. Abimelech destroys Shechem, sows it with salt, and burns about a thousand people in the stronghold of the house of Elberith. At Thebez a woman drops a millstone on his head, he has his armor bearer kill him, and the text says God repaid the wickedness of Abimelech and Shechem as Jotham cursed.

l: Abimelech, The Book of Judges, Chapter 9
s: Abimelech, Jerubbaal's son by a female servant, gains Shechem's support, hires reckless men, kills his seventy brothers, and is made king. After three years Shechem betrays him; he defeats Gaal, destroys Shechem and burns its tower's people, then attacks Thebez. A woman's millstone breaks his skull and he has his armor bearer kill him so it won't be said a woman killed him.

l: Gideon, The Book of Judges, Chapter 9
s: Jerubbaal is the father of seventy sons and of Abimelech. Jotham says he fought for Shechem, risked his life, and delivered them from Midian, yet his house was repaid with the killing of his sons.

l: house of Jerubbaal, The Book of Judges, Chapter 9
s: The seventy sons of Jerubbaal are killed by Abimelech on one stone at Ophrah. Only the youngest, Jotham, survives. Their blood is said to be laid on Abimelech and the men of Shechem.

l: Jotham, The Book of Judges, Chapter 9
s: Jotham, Jerubbaal's youngest son, hides and survives the massacre. From Mount Gerizim he tells the parable of the trees and calls down fire on Abimelech and Shechem, then flees to Beer for fear of Abimelech. The text closes by saying his curse came on them.

l: men of Shechem, The Book of Judges, Chapter 9
s: The men of Shechem follow Abimelech because he is their brother, fund his killers from the house of Baal Berith, and make him king. After God sends an evil spirit, they betray him with ambushes and trust Gaal. Abimelech kills them, and about a thousand die in the burned stronghold.

l: Shechem, The Book of Judges, Chapter 9
s: Shechem is where Abimelech is made king by the oak of the pillar. Zebul drives Gaal out of it, and Abimelech fights against it all day, takes it, kills its people, beats it down, and sows it with salt.

l: parable of the trees, The Book of Judges, Chapter 9
s: In Jotham's parable the olive, fig, and vine each refuse to reign over the trees, unwilling to give up their oil, fruit, and wine. The bramble accepts, offering shade and threatening fire to devour the cedars of Lebanon. Jotham applies it to Abimelech and Shechem.

l: LORD, The Book of Judges, Chapter 9
s: God sends an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem so that the violence done to the seventy sons would be repaid. The text states that God repaid the wickedness of Abimelech and of the men of Shechem on their heads.

l: Gaal, The Book of Judges, Chapter 9
s: Gaal son of Ebed comes to Shechem with his brothers and wins the men's trust. He mocks Abimelech and wishes to remove him, but Zebul taunts him, he loses the fight, and Zebul drives him and his brothers out of Shechem.

l: Zebul, The Book of Judges, Chapter 9
s: Zebul, ruler of the city, grows angry at Gaal's words and secretly sends word to Abimelech to ambush. He taunts Gaal into going out to fight and afterward drives Gaal and his brothers out of Shechem.

l: Thebez, The Book of Judges, Chapter 9
s: Abimelech camps against Thebez and takes it. The people flee into a strong tower within the city, and during his attack on its door a woman's millstone kills him.

l: woman of Thebez, The Book of Judges, Chapter 9
s: A certain woman on the tower roof at Thebez casts an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and breaks his skull. This leads to his death.

l: destruction of Shechem, The Book of Judges, Chapter 9
s: Abimelech divides his people into companies, strikes those coming out of the city, fights all day, takes the city, kills its people, beats it down, and sows it with salt. He then burns the stronghold of the house of Elberith over the men of the tower, killing about a thousand men and women.

l: Jotham's curse, The Book of Judges, Chapter 9
s: Jotham prays that fire come out from Abimelech to devour Shechem and from Shechem to devour Abimelech if they have not dealt rightly with Jerubbaal's house. The chapter ends by saying the curse came on the men of Shechem, as Abimelech and Shechem destroy each other.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 10
s: Chapter 10 records two judges: Tola of Issachar, who judged Israel twenty-three years and was buried in Shamir, and Jair the Gileadite, who judged twenty-two years, had thirty sons and thirty cities, and was buried in Kamon. Israel then again did evil, serving the Baals, Ashtaroth and the gods of many neighboring peoples, and abandoned the LORD. In anger the LORD sold them into the hands of the Philistines and the Ammonites, who oppressed them for eighteen years, including beyond the Jordan in Gilead. Israel cried out and confessed sin; the LORD reminded them of his past rescues and told them to cry to their chosen gods, but they put away the foreign gods and served him, and his soul was grieved by their misery. The Ammonites encamped in Gilead, Israel assembled at Mizpah, and the princes of Gilead offered headship over Gilead to whoever would begin the fight.

l: Jair, The Book of Judges, Chapter 10
s: Jair the Gileadite arose after Tola and judged Israel twenty-two years. He had thirty sons who rode thirty donkey colts and held thirty cities, called Havvoth Jair to this day in Gilead. He died and was buried in Kamon.

l: Gilead, The Book of Judges, Chapter 10
s: Gilead is the land of Jair's thirty cities, called Havvoth Jair. It was where the Amorites lived and where Israelites beyond the Jordan were oppressed for eighteen years. The Ammonites encamped there, and its princes offered headship over all Gilead's inhabitants to whoever would begin the fight against them.

l: Israel, The Book of Judges, Chapter 10
s: Israel was led by Tola for twenty-three years and Jair for twenty-two years, then again did evil and was sold to the Philistines and Ammonites. It cried out, confessed its sin, put away the foreign gods and served the LORD. It then assembled at Mizpah against the Ammonites.

l: LORD, The Book of Judges, Chapter 10
s: The LORD, angered by Israel's idolatry, sold them into the hands of the Philistines and Ammonites. He recounted how he had saved them from the Egyptians, Amorites, Ammonites, Philistines, Sidonians, Amalekites and Maonites, and said he would save them no more, telling them to cry to their chosen gods. When they put away the foreign gods, his soul was grieved for their misery.

l: children of Ammon, The Book of Judges, Chapter 10
s: The Ammonites, with the Philistines, oppressed Israel for eighteen years after the LORD sold Israel into their hands. They crossed the Jordan to fight Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim, leaving Israel very distressed. They then gathered and encamped in Gilead.

l: Israel's sin and idolatry (Israel), The Book of Judges, Chapter 10
s: Israel again did evil, serving the Baals, the Ashtaroth and the gods of Syria, Sidon, Moab, Ammon and the Philistines, and abandoned the LORD. They confessed having forsaken God, and the LORD said he would save them no more and told them to cry to their chosen gods. Israel then admitted its sin, asked for deliverance, and put away the foreign gods to serve the LORD.

l: Ammonite oppression (Israel), The Book of Judges, Chapter 10
s: Because of the LORD's anger, Israel was sold into the hands of the Philistines and Ammonites, who oppressed them for eighteen years, especially those beyond the Jordan in Gilead. The Ammonites crossed the Jordan to fight Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim, leaving Israel very distressed. The oppression led Israel to cry to the LORD and ended with the Ammonites encamped in Gilead and Israel at Mizpah.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 11
s: Jephthah the Gileadite, a mighty man of valor and the son of a prostitute, is driven out by Gilead's other sons and flees to the land of Tob. When the children of Ammon make war on Israel, the elders of Gilead bring him back and make him head and chief over Gilead. Jephthah sends messengers to the king of the children of Ammon, rebutting the claim to the land by recounting Israel's history with Edom, Moab, and Sihon the Amorite, but the king does not listen. After the LORD's Spirit comes on him, Jephthah vows that whatever first comes out of his house to meet him will be the LORD's burnt offering, and the LORD delivers Ammon into his hand. His only child, his daughter, comes out to meet him; she tells him to do as he vowed, mourns her virginity on the mountains for two months, and then he does with her according to his vow, after which Israel's daughters yearly celebrate her four days a year.

l: Jephthah the Gileadite, The Book of Judges, Chapter 11
s: Jephthah, son of Gilead and a prostitute, is driven out by his half-brothers, lives in Tob with outlaws, and is recalled by the elders to be head and chief of Gilead. He argues Israel's case to the Ammonite king, makes a vow to the LORD, defeats Ammon, and then, upon his only daughter coming out to meet him, tears his clothes and carries out his vow.

l: elders of Gilead, The Book of Judges, Chapter 11
s: The elders of Gilead, who had earlier hated Jephthah and driven him out, go to Tob to fetch him when Ammon makes war. They promise him headship over all the inhabitants of Gilead, call the LORD witness between them, and the people make him head and chief.

l: children of Ammon, The Book of Judges, Chapter 11
s: The children of Ammon make war against Israel and are the object of Jephthah's vow. After their king ignores Jephthah's message, the LORD delivers them into Jephthah's hand, and he strikes them from Aroer to Minnith, twenty cities, and to Abelcheramim with great slaughter, so they are subdued before Israel.

l: king of the children of Ammon, The Book of Judges, Chapter 11
s: The king claims that Israel took Ammon's land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and the Jordan when it came out of Egypt, and demands its peaceable return. Jephthah replies twice with historical arguments, but the king does not listen to his words.

l: Israel, The Book of Judges, Chapter 11
s: Israel is attacked by the children of Ammon and defended by Jephthah's account of its history: refused passage by Edom and Moab, it went around them, and after Sihon the Amorite fought it, the LORD gave it his land. Israel is said to have lived in Heshbon, Aroer, and the Arnon cities for three hundred years, and its daughters came to celebrate Jephthah's daughter yearly for four days.

l: LORD, The Book of Judges, Chapter 11
s: The LORD is called witness between Jephthah and the elders and Judge between Israel and Ammon. His Spirit comes on Jephthah, he delivers Ammon into Jephthah's hand, and Jephthah says he delivered Sihon and the Amorites to Israel and dispossessed the Amorites before his people.

l: Jephthah's vow, The Book of Judges, Chapter 11
s: Jephthah vows that if the LORD delivers Ammon into his hand, whatever comes out of his house doors to meet him on his peaceful return will be the LORD's and he will offer it as a burnt offering. The LORD grants the victory, his daughter is the first to come out, and Jephthah says he cannot go back on what he has said to the LORD; he does with her according to the vow.

l: Jephthah's daughter, The Book of Judges, Chapter 11
s: Jephthah's only child, she comes out to meet him with tambourines and dances after his victory. She tells him to do to her what he has vowed, asks two months with her companions on the mountains to mourn her virginity, then returns, and her father does with her according to his vow. She is remembered by a yearly four-day celebration by the daughters of Israel.

l: Ammonite oppression (Israel), The Book of Judges, Chapter 11
s: The war begins when the children of Ammon make war on Israel, claiming land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and the Jordan. After diplomatic exchanges fail, Jephthah crosses Gilead, Manasseh, and Mizpah to reach Ammon, and the LORD delivers Ammon to him, resulting in a great slaughter and Ammon's subjugation.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 12
s: The men of Ephraim confront Jephthah for not summoning them to fight the children of Ammon and threaten to burn his house. Jephthah answers that they failed to save him when he called, so he risked his life and the LORD delivered the Ammonites to him. He gathers the men of Gilead and fights Ephraim, seizing the fords of the Jordan and killing anyone who cannot pronounce 'Shibboleth' correctly, and forty-two thousand of Ephraim fall. Jephthah judges Israel six years and is buried in the cities of Gilead. Ibzan of Bethlehem, Elon the Zebulunite, and Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite then judge Israel for seven, ten, and eight years respectively, each dying and being buried in his own place.

l: Jephthah the Gileadite, The Book of Judges, Chapter 12
s: Jephthah is threatened by the men of Ephraim for not calling them to fight Ammon, and he replies that they did not save him when he called. He gathers the men of Gilead and fights Ephraim. He judges Israel six years, then dies and is buried in the cities of Gilead.

l: Ephraim, The Book of Judges, Chapter 12
s: The men of Ephraim gather, pass northward, and threaten to burn Jephthah's house because he did not call them to fight Ammon. They are struck by the men of Gilead, and fugitives are killed at the Jordan fords when they cannot say 'Shibboleth' correctly. Forty-two thousand of Ephraim fall.

l: men of Gilead, The Book of Judges, Chapter 12
s: The men of Gilead are gathered by Jephthah and fight and strike Ephraim, after saying Ephraim's people are fugitives in the middle of Ephraim and Manasseh. They take the fords of the Jordan and test those crossing by asking whether they are Ephraimites and having them say 'Shibboleth'. Those who fail are seized and killed.

l: children of Ammon, The Book of Judges, Chapter 12
s: The children of Ammon are recalled by Jephthah as those with whom he and his people were in great strife. He says he passed over against them and the LORD delivered them into his hand.

l: Jordan, The Book of Judges, Chapter 12
s: The Gileadites take the fords of the Jordan against the Ephraimites. Fugitives of Ephraim who try to cross are questioned and killed there if they fail the pronunciation test.

l: Shibboleth, The Book of Judges, Chapter 12
s: 'Shibboleth' is the word the Gileadites make suspected Ephraimites say at the Jordan fords. Those who say 'Sibboleth' because they cannot pronounce it correctly are seized and killed.

l: Ibzan, The Book of Judges, Chapter 12
s: Ibzan of Bethlehem judges Israel after Jephthah. He has thirty sons and thirty daughters, sending his daughters outside his clan and bringing in thirty daughters from outside for his sons. He judges seven years, then dies and is buried at Bethlehem.

l: Elon, The Book of Judges, Chapter 12
s: Elon the Zebulunite judges Israel after Ibzan for ten years. He dies and is buried in Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.

l: Abdon, The Book of Judges, Chapter 12
s: Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite judges Israel after Elon for eight years. He has forty sons and thirty sons' sons who ride on seventy donkey colts. He dies and is buried in Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.

l: battle between Gilead and Ephraim, The Book of Judges, Chapter 12
s: After Ephraim threatens Jephthah, he gathers the men of Gilead and fights Ephraim, who are struck down. The Gileadites hold the Jordan fords and kill fugitives who fail the 'Shibboleth' test. Forty-two thousand of Ephraim fall.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 13
s: After the children of Israel again did evil, the LORD delivered them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years. The LORD's angel appeared to the barren wife of Manoah, a Danite of Zorah, and told her she would bear a son who would be a Nazirite to God and begin to save Israel from the Philistines. Manoah prayed for the man of God to return, and the angel came again, repeated his instructions, declined Manoah's food, and told him to offer a burnt offering to the LORD. When the angel ascended in the flame of the altar, Manoah realized who he was and feared they would die, but his wife reasoned that the LORD's acceptance of the offering showed otherwise. She bore a son, Samson, whom the LORD blessed and whose Spirit began to move him in Mahaneh Dan.

l: Manoah, The Book of Judges, Chapter 13
s: Manoah, a Danite man of Zorah, prayed that the man of God would return to teach them how to raise the promised child. He questioned the angel, offered him a young goat, asked his name, and then made a burnt offering to the LORD. After the angel ascended in the flame, he realized who he was and feared they would die, but his wife reassured him.

l: wife of Manoah, The Book of Judges, Chapter 13
s: The barren and childless wife of Manoah was told by the LORD's angel that she would conceive and bear a son, and she was told to avoid wine, strong drink, and unclean food. She reported the encounter to her husband and ran to fetch him when the angel reappeared. She calmed his fear of death by arguing that the LORD would not have accepted their offering or shown them these things if he meant to kill them, and she then bore Samson.

l: angel of the LORD (messenger to Manoah and his wife), The Book of Judges, Chapter 13
s: The angel appeared to Manoah's wife, announced the birth of a Nazirite son who would begin to save Israel from the Philistines, and later returned and repeated his commands to Manoah. He refused to eat Manoah's food, told him to offer a burnt offering to the LORD, and declined to give his name because it is incomprehensible. He ascended in the altar flame and did not appear again, after which Manoah knew who he was.

l: LORD, The Book of Judges, Chapter 13
s: The LORD delivered the children of Israel into the hand of the Philistines for forty years because of their evil. He sent his angel to announce Samson's birth, heard Manoah's prayer, and received the burnt and meal offerings. He blessed the child Samson, and his Spirit began to move him.

l: Samson, The Book of Judges, Chapter 13
s: Samson was promised before his conception as a Nazirite to God from the womb who would begin to save Israel from the Philistines. He was born to Manoah's wife and named Samson, grew, and was blessed by the LORD. The LORD's Spirit began to move him in Mahaneh Dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.

l: Israel, The Book of Judges, Chapter 13
s: The children of Israel again did evil in the LORD's sight. As a result, the LORD delivered them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years.

l: Philistines, The Book of Judges, Chapter 13
s: The Philistines held the children of Israel under their power for forty years by the LORD's act of delivering Israel to them. The angel announced that Samson would begin to save Israel from their hand.

l: Nazirite vow, The Book of Judges, Chapter 13
s: The angel declared that the promised child would be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death. This meant no razor on his head, and his mother was to drink no wine or strong drink and eat nothing unclean, nor anything that comes of the vine.

l: burnt offering (Manoah's offering), The Book of Judges, Chapter 13
s: At the angel's direction, Manoah offered a young goat with a meal offering on the rock to the LORD. As the flame rose from the altar, the angel ascended in it while Manoah and his wife watched and fell on their faces. Manoah's wife later cited the LORD's acceptance of this offering as evidence that he did not intend to kill them.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 14
s: Samson sees a Philistine woman in Timnah and asks his parents to get her for him as his wife, despite their objection; the narrator says the matter was of the LORD, who sought an occasion against the Philistines. On the way to Timnah, Samson tears apart a young lion with the LORD's Spirit on him, and later finds bees and honey in its carcass, eating the honey and sharing it with his parents without telling them its source. At his wedding feast he poses a riddle about the lion and honey to thirty companions, wagering thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothing. The companions threaten Samson's wife, she weeps until he tells her the answer, and she reveals it to them, so they answer him on the seventh day. Samson, with the LORD's Spirit on him, goes to Ashkelon, kills thirty men and pays the garments with their plunder, then goes angrily to his father's house, and his wife is given to his companion.

l: Samson, The Book of Judges, Chapter 14
s: Samson sees a Philistine woman in Timnah and insists his parents get her for him as wife. He kills a lion bare-handed, eats honey from its carcass, and poses a riddle at his feast. After his wife betrays the answer, he kills thirty men at Ashkelon to pay his wager and returns angrily to his father's house, losing his wife to his companion.

l: Samson's wife, The Book of Judges, Chapter 14
s: She is a Philistine woman from Timnah whom Samson finds pleasing and marries. Pressured by threats of burning from the thirty companions, she weeps for seven days until Samson tells her the riddle, and she tells it to her people. She is then given to Samson's companion who had been his friend.

l: Timnah, The Book of Judges, Chapter 14
s: Timnah is where Samson sees and later talks with the Philistine woman he wants as wife. Its vineyards are where the young lion roars at him, and it is the place of the marriage feast.

l: Philistines, The Book of Judges, Chapter 14
s: The Philistines are described as uncircumcised and as ruling over Israel at that time. Samson's parents object to his taking a wife from among them, but the LORD is said to be seeking an occasion against them. Samson later strikes thirty men in Ashkelon.

l: LORD, The Book of Judges, Chapter 14
s: The narrator says Samson's desire for the Philistine woman was of the LORD, who sought an occasion against the Philistines. The LORD's Spirit comes mightily on Samson when he tears the lion and again when he goes to Ashkelon and strikes thirty men.

l: young lion (Samson's kill), The Book of Judges, Chapter 14
s: A young lion roars at Samson in the vineyards of Timnah, and he tears it apart with his bare hands as if it were a young goat, by the LORD's Spirit. Its carcass later holds a swarm of bees and honey, which become the basis of his riddle.

l: bees and honey (in the lion's carcass), The Book of Judges, Chapter 14
s: Samson finds a swarm of bees and honey in the lion's carcass. He eats the honey as he goes and gives some to his parents without telling them where it came from. This secret is the hidden answer to his riddle.

l: wedding feast (Samson's feast), The Book of Judges, Chapter 14
s: Samson holds a feast in Timnah, as young men used to do, and thirty companions are brought to be with him. It lasts seven days, during which he poses his riddle and his wife weeps to learn its answer.

l: thirty companions (at Samson's feast), The Book of Judges, Chapter 14
s: Thirty companions are brought to be with Samson at his feast. They cannot solve his riddle in three days, so on the seventh day they threaten Samson's wife with burning to make her get the answer. They then answer the riddle before sunset and receive the garments Samson pays from the plunder at Ashkelon.

l: riddle (Samson's riddle), The Book of Judges, Chapter 14
s: Samson's riddle is: "Out of the eater came out food. Out of the strong came out sweetness." The companions fail for three days, then learn the answer through his wife and reply, "What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?" Samson says they have plowed with his heifer.

l: wager garments (thirty linen garments and changes of clothing), The Book of Judges, Chapter 14
s: Samson stakes thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothing on the riddle, with the same owed to him if the companions fail. When they answer correctly, he pays the changes of clothing to them, taking them as plunder from the thirty men he strikes at Ashkelon.

l: Ashkelon, The Book of Judges, Chapter 14
s: Ashkelon is where Samson goes down after the companions answer his riddle, with the LORD's Spirit on him. There he strikes thirty men and takes their plunder.

l: thirty men of Ashkelon, The Book of Judges, Chapter 14
s: Thirty men of Ashkelon are struck by Samson. He takes their plunder and uses the changes of clothing to pay those who declared his riddle.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 15
s: In Judges 15, Samson comes to visit his wife at harvest time but her father refuses him entry, having given her to Samson's companion. Samson retaliates by tying torches to the tails of three hundred foxes and loosing them to burn the Philistines' grain and olive groves; the Philistines respond by burning his wife and her father, and Samson strikes them with great slaughter and takes refuge in the cave in Etam's rock. The Philistines then camp at Lehi in Judah, and three thousand men of Judah bind Samson with two new ropes to hand him over. At Lehi the LORD's Spirit comes on Samson, he breaks the ropes, and with a fresh donkey's jawbone he strikes a thousand men. Thirsty, he calls on the LORD, God splits the hollow place in Lehi so water comes out, and the narrator notes that Samson judged Israel twenty years in the days of the Philistines.

l: Samson, The Book of Judges, Chapter 15
s: Samson visits his wife at wheat harvest with a young goat but is refused entry, then burns the Philistines' crops with foxes and strikes them hip and thigh in revenge for her death. He is bound by the men of Judah, breaks free when the LORD's Spirit comes on him, kills a thousand men with a donkey's jawbone, and is revived by water God provides. He is said to have judged Israel twenty years in the days of the Philistines.

l: Samson's wife, The Book of Judges, Chapter 15
s: Samson's wife has been given by her father to Samson's companion, and Samson is not allowed to see her. The Philistines later burn her with fire, because Samson's act of burning their crops is blamed on his having had her taken and given away.

l: father of Samson's wife, The Book of Judges, Chapter 15
s: He refuses to let Samson into his daughter's room, saying he thought Samson utterly hated her and so gave her to Samson's companion. He offers Samson her younger sister instead, and is later burned with fire by the Philistines along with his daughter.

l: Philistines, The Book of Judges, Chapter 15
s: The Philistines lose their grain and olive groves to Samson's fire and respond by burning Samson's wife and her father. They then encamp in Judah and spread out in Lehi to bind Samson, and shout as they meet him, but Samson breaks his bonds and strikes a thousand of them. They are described as rulers over Judah.

l: men of Judah, The Book of Judges, Chapter 15
s: Three thousand men of Judah go down to the cave in Etam's rock to bind Samson and deliver him to the Philistines, reminding him that the Philistines rule over them. They get his agreement not to be attacked by them, bind him with two new ropes, promise not to kill him, and bring him up from the rock to Lehi.

l: foxes (Samson's three hundred foxes), The Book of Judges, Chapter 15
s: Samson catches three hundred foxes, turns them tail to tail, and puts a torch between every two tails. Once the torches are lit, he lets the foxes go into the Philistines' standing grain.

l: Philistine crops (standing grain, shocks, olive groves), The Book of Judges, Chapter 15
s: The standing grain, the shocks, and the olive groves of the Philistines are set ablaze by the torch-carrying foxes and burned up.

l: burning of the Philistine crops, The Book of Judges, Chapter 15
s: Samson does this in retaliation after his wife is given to his companion, saying he will be blameless in the case of the Philistines when he harms them. It prompts the Philistines to ask who did it and to burn Samson's wife and her father in response.

l: cave in Etam's rock, The Book of Judges, Chapter 15
s: After striking the Philistines with great slaughter, Samson goes down and lives in the cave in Etam's rock. The men of Judah come to it to bind him, and he is brought up from the rock bound with two new ropes.

l: Lehi, The Book of Judges, Chapter 15
s: The Philistines spread themselves in Lehi after encamping in Judah. Samson is brought there bound, breaks free, and strikes a thousand men with a jawbone. The place where he throws the jawbone is called Ramath Lehi, and God splits the hollow place in Lehi to give him water.

l: jawbone of a donkey, The Book of Judges, Chapter 15
s: Samson finds a fresh donkey's jawbone, takes it, and strikes a thousand men with it, then composes a verse about it. He throws it out of his hand when he finishes speaking, and the place is called Ramath Lehi.

l: Samson's slaughter of a thousand men, The Book of Judges, Chapter 15
s: At Lehi, after breaking his bonds, Samson strikes a thousand men with a fresh donkey's jawbone. He commemorates it saying, 'heaps on heaps; with the jawbone of a donkey I have struck a thousand men.'

l: LORD, The Book of Judges, Chapter 15
s: The LORD's Spirit comes mightily on Samson at Lehi so that his ropes become like burned flax and fall from his hands. When Samson calls on the LORD in thirst, calling the victory a great deliverance by his servant's hand, God splits the hollow place in Lehi and water comes out, reviving him.

l: En Hakkore, The Book of Judges, Chapter 15
s: En Hakkore is the name given to the spring of water that comes out of the hollow place God splits in Lehi after Samson prays. The text says it bears this name to this day.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 16
s: Samson visits a prostitute in Gaza, and the Gazites lie in wait to kill him, but he rises at midnight and carries off the city gate doors, posts and all, to a mountain before Hebron. He then loves Delilah of the valley of Sorek, and the lords of the Philistines offer her eleven hundred pieces of silver each to learn the source of his strength. After three false answers that she tests on him, Delilah presses him daily until he reveals he is a Nazirite whose strength depends on never being shaved. She has his seven locks shaved while he sleeps on her knees, and the Philistines seize him, put out his eyes, and set him to grind at the mill in the prison in Gaza. At a sacrifice to Dagon, with his hair growing back, Samson is brought out to entertain them, prays to the LORD for strength, pulls down the two middle pillars, and kills more people in his death than in his life; his family buries him between Zorah and Eshtaol, and the text says he judged Israel twenty years.

l: Samson, The Book of Judges, Chapter 16
s: Samson goes in to a prostitute in Gaza, escapes an ambush by carrying off the city gate, and loves Delilah. After deceiving her three times, he tells her the secret of his Nazirite hair, is shaved, blinded, bound in bronze fetters and made to grind at the prison mill. He later prays to the LORD, brings down the house of Dagon on himself and the Philistines, and is buried in his father's burial site, having judged Israel twenty years.

l: Delilah, The Book of Judges, Chapter 16
s: Delilah, a woman Samson loves in the valley of Sorek, is offered eleven hundred pieces of silver by each of the lords of the Philistines to discover the source of his strength. She tests three false answers on him, presses him daily until he tells all, then calls the lords, has his seven locks shaved while he sleeps on her knees, and begins to afflict him.

l: lords of the Philistines, The Book of Judges, Chapter 16
s: The lords of the Philistines come up to Delilah and promise each to give her eleven hundred pieces of silver if she learns Samson's secret. They bring seven green cords, then come again with the money after she says he has told all. They gather to sacrifice to Dagon and are present in the house when it falls on them.

l: Philistines, The Book of Judges, Chapter 16
s: The Philistines are the people whom Delilah falsely announces are upon Samson, and who later seize him, put out his eyes, take him to Gaza and bind him in bronze fetters. They credit Dagon with delivering Samson, their enemy, into their hands, and call him to entertain them. Samson avenges himself on them as the house collapses, killing more of them in his death than in his life.

l: LORD, The Book of Judges, Chapter 16
s: The LORD has departed from Samson without his knowing it when he wakes after being shaved. Samson later calls on the LORD as Lord GOD to remember and strengthen him once more so he may be avenged on the Philistines for his two eyes, and he then takes hold of the pillars.

l: Nazirite vow, The Book of Judges, Chapter 16
s: Samson tells Delilah that no razor has ever come on his head because he has been a Nazirite to God from his mother's womb. He says that if he is shaved his strength will leave him and he will become like any other man.

l: Samson's hair, The Book of Judges, Chapter 16
s: Samson's seven locks are woven into a loom in a false test, but he plucks out the pin. Delilah has a man shave them off while he sleeps, and his strength goes. His hair begins to grow again after the shaving.

l: Samson's strength, The Book of Judges, Chapter 16
s: Samson's strength lets him carry the Gaza gate doors with the posts to a mountain before Hebron and break green cords, new ropes and a loom pin. It leaves him when his locks are shaved, and he does not know the LORD has departed. He asks the LORD to strengthen him this once, and with it he bows the pillars.

l: house of Dagon, The Book of Judges, Chapter 16
s: The house is where the Philistine lords gather to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god, rejoicing that he has delivered Samson. It is full of men and women, with about three thousand more on the roof watching Samson perform. It falls on the lords and all the people in it.

l: pillars (of the house), The Book of Judges, Chapter 16
s: Samson is set between the pillars and asks the boy holding his hand to let him feel the pillars on which the house rests so he can lean on them. He takes hold of the two middle pillars, one with each hand, and bows with all his might.

l: Samson's death and the collapse of the house, The Book of Judges, Chapter 16
s: Samson says, "Let me die with the Philistines!" and bows himself, and the house falls on the lords and all the people in it. The dead he kills at his death outnumber those he killed in his life. His brothers and his father's house bring him up and bury him between Zorah and Eshtaol in Manoah's burial site.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 17
s: Chapter 17 introduces Micah, a man of the hill country of Ephraim, who confesses to his mother that he took her eleven hundred pieces of silver, which she had cursed. He returns it, and she dedicates it to the LORD for a carved image and a molten image, for which she gives two hundred pieces to a silversmith. Micah keeps a house of gods, makes an ephod and teraphim, and consecrates one of his sons as priest. The text notes that there was no king in Israel and everyone did what was right in his own eyes. A young Levite from Bethlehem Judah, seeking a place to live, arrives at Micah's house, and Micah hires him as priest for ten pieces of silver per year, clothing, and food, then declares that the LORD will do him good because he has a Levite as priest.

l: Micah, The Book of Judges, Chapter 17
s: Micah, a man of the hill country of Ephraim, admits to his mother that he took her eleven hundred pieces of silver and returns it. He keeps a house of gods with an image, an ephod, and teraphim, and first consecrates one of his sons as priest. He then hires a wandering Levite as his priest, believing that the LORD will now do him good.

l: Micah's mother, The Book of Judges, Chapter 17
s: Micah's mother had lost eleven hundred pieces of silver and uttered a curse about it. When her son confesses and returns it, she blesses him in the LORD's name and dedicates the silver to the LORD for a carved image and a molten image. She gives two hundred pieces to a silversmith.

l: eleven hundred pieces of silver, The Book of Judges, Chapter 17
s: The eleven hundred pieces of silver were taken from Micah's mother, who cursed the theft, and Micah admits he took them. He restores them, and his mother dedicates them to the LORD for making images. Two hundred pieces are given to a silversmith to make the carved image and molten image.

l: carved image and molten image (Micah's), The Book of Judges, Chapter 17
s: A silversmith makes a carved image and a molten image from two hundred of the pieces of silver, and they are placed in Micah's house. They form part of Micah's house of gods, along with an ephod and teraphim.

l: Levite (young man of Bethlehem Judah), The Book of Judges, Chapter 17
s: A young Levite from Bethlehem Judah, of the family of Judah, leaves the city to find a place to live and comes to Micah's house in Ephraim. Micah invites him to be a father and priest for ten pieces of silver per year, a suit of clothing, and food. The Levite is content, is treated as one of Micah's sons, and is consecrated as his priest.

l: priesthood arrangement (Micah and the Levite), The Book of Judges, Chapter 17
s: Micah offers the Levite a position as father and priest in exchange for ten pieces of silver per year, a suit of clothing, and his food, and the Levite accepts. Micah consecrates him, replacing the earlier arrangement in which one of his sons was priest. Micah then says he knows the LORD will do him good because he has a Levite as priest.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 18
s: The tribe of Dan, lacking an inheritance, sends five men to spy out the land; at Micah's house in the hill country of Ephraim they recognize the young Levite and ask him to seek counsel from God, and he tells them their way is before the LORD. The five find Laish, a quiet, secure people far from the Sidonians, and urge their brothers to attack. Six hundred armed Danites travel to Micah's house, where the five take the engraved image, ephod, teraphim, and molten image, and the priest agrees to go with them. Micah pursues but retreats when threatened, and the Danites strike Laish with the sword, burn it, and rebuild it as Dan. They set up Micah's engraved image, with Jonathan son of Gershom, son of Moses, and his sons as priests.

l: Danites, The Book of Judges, Chapter 18
s: The Danites, lacking an inheritance among the tribes, sent five men to spy out the land, then set out with six hundred armed men. They seized Micah's image, ephod, and teraphim, took his priest, and threatened Micah when he protested. They struck Laish with the sword, burned it, rebuilt it and named it Dan, and set up the engraved image, with Jonathan and his sons as priests.

l: five men, The Book of Judges, Chapter 18
s: The five men, valiant men of Dan from Zorah and Eshtaol, were sent to spy out the land and lodged at Micah's house, where they recognized the Levite and asked him for counsel. They saw Laish's people living in safety and urged their brothers to attack. On the return they told the six hundred about the ephod and images in Micah's house and went in and took them.

l: Micah, The Book of Judges, Chapter 18
s: Micah had hired the young Levite as his priest and kept an ephod, teraphim, a carved image, and a molten image in his house. When the Danites took the images and the priest, he protested that they had taken his gods and the priest, leaving him with nothing. After the Danites warned that angry men might take his life and his household's, and he saw they were too strong, he went back home.

l: Levite (young man of Bethlehem Judah), The Book of Judges, Chapter 18
s: The young Levite was recognized by the five men, who asked how he came to be there. He explained that Micah had hired him, and told them their way was before the LORD. When the Danites invited him to be priest to a tribe rather than one man's house, his heart was glad and he took the ephod, teraphim, and engraved image and went with them. He is identified as Jonathan, son of Gershom, son of Moses, who with his sons served as priests to the Danites until the captivity of the land.

l: Laish, The Book of Judges, Chapter 18
s: Laish was a city in a valley by Beth Rehob, far from Sidon, which the five men found quiet and secure with no one holding authority over it. It had no deliverer and was struck with the sword and burned by the Danites. They rebuilt it and renamed it Dan after their father.

l: people of Laish, The Book of Judges, Chapter 18
s: The people of Laish lived quiet and unsuspecting, in the way of the Sidonians, with no dealings with anyone else. The spies described them as an unsuspecting people in a land lacking nothing. The Danites struck them with the edge of the sword, and no one came to deliver them because they were far from Sidon.

l: carved image and molten image (Micah's), The Book of Judges, Chapter 18
s: Micah's ephod, teraphim, engraved image, and molten image were pointed out by the five men to the six hundred. The five men took them from Micah's house while the priest stood at the gate with the armed men. The Danites carried them to Laish and set up the engraved image for themselves, where it remained all the time God's house was in Shiloh.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 19
s: A Levite from the far side of the hill country of Ephraim goes to Bethlehem Judah to bring back his concubine, who had left him, and her father keeps delaying their departure for several days. The Levite finally leaves late in the day with his servant, the concubine, and two donkeys, refuses to lodge in the Jebusite city, and stops at Gibeah of Benjamin, where an old man from Ephraim takes them in. Wicked men of the city surround the house and demand the Levite be brought out for sex; the old man offers his virgin daughter and the concubine instead, and the Levite pushes his concubine out to them. They rape and abuse her all night, and she collapses at the door, and in the morning the Levite finds her, takes her home on the donkey, cuts her into twelve pieces, and sends them throughout Israel. All who see it say nothing like it has happened since Israel left Egypt and call for consideration and counsel.

l: Levite (the concubine's husband), The Book of Judges, Chapter 19
s: The Levite goes to Bethlehem Judah to speak kindly to his concubine and bring her back, stays several days with her father, and then leaves in the evening, refusing to lodge in a foreign city and choosing Gibeah. At the old man's house he gives his concubine to the men of the city, then finds her fallen at the door, takes her home, cuts her into twelve pieces, and sends them throughout Israel.

l: concubine (the Levite's concubine), The Book of Judges, Chapter 19
s: The concubine had played the prostitute against the Levite and gone to her father's house in Bethlehem Judah, where she stayed four months before he came for her. At Gibeah she is pushed out to the mob, raped and abused all night, and collapses at the door with her hands on the threshold; she does not answer the Levite, and he cuts her body into twelve pieces.

l: father-in-law (the concubine's father), The Book of Judges, Chapter 19
s: The young woman's father rejoices to see the Levite and keeps him in his house, urging him with food, drink, and merriment to stay through several days. His repeated urging delays the Levite's departure until the day is nearly over on the fifth day.

l: old man (of Gibeah), The Book of Judges, Chapter 19
s: An old man from the hill country of Ephraim, living in Gibeah, sees the travelers in the street, offers to supply all their needs, and takes them into his house. When the men of the city demand the Levite, he pleads with them not to act wickedly and offers his virgin daughter and the Levite's concubine instead.

l: men of Gibeah (wicked fellows), The Book of Judges, Chapter 19
s: Wicked men of the city surround the old man's house, beat at the door, and demand that the Levite be brought out so they can have sex with him. They refuse the old man's plea, take the concubine, rape and abuse her all night, and let her go at dawn.

l: Israel, The Book of Judges, Chapter 19
s: The chapter opens by noting there was no king in Israel. The Levite sends pieces of his concubine's body throughout all of Israel's borders, and everyone who sees them says no such deed has been done since Israel came up out of Egypt, urging that it be considered, counsel taken, and a word spoken.

l: Bethlehem Judah, The Book of Judges, Chapter 19
s: Bethlehem Judah is where the Levite takes his concubine from and where her father's house is, to which she returns for four months. The Levite stays there several days before leaving for the hill country of Ephraim.

l: Gibeah, The Book of Judges, Chapter 19
s: Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin, is where the Levite's party stops at sundown after passing by Jebus, and no one there takes them in until an Ephraimite old man does. Its inhabitants are Benjamites, and the men of the city commit the assault on the concubine there.

l: gang rape and abuse of the concubine, The Book of Judges, Chapter 19
s: After the Levite brings his concubine out to the mob at the old man's door, the men of Gibeah rape and abuse her all night until dawn. She then falls at the door of the house and does not answer when the Levite tells her to get up.

l: dismemberment of the concubine, The Book of Judges, Chapter 19
s: At his home, the Levite takes a knife, cuts his concubine limb by limb into twelve pieces, and sends them throughout the borders of Israel. Those who see it declare that nothing like it has been done or seen since Israel left Egypt and call for consideration and counsel.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 20
s: All the children of Israel assemble at Mizpah, where the Levite recounts how the men of Gibeah attacked him and raped his concubine, who died, and how he cut her in pieces and sent her throughout Israel. Israel vows to punish Gibeah and demands that Benjamin hand over the wicked men, but Benjamin refuses and musters twenty-six thousand swordsmen plus seven hundred chosen men of Gibeah. Benjamin defeats Israel on two days, killing twenty-two thousand and then eighteen thousand, even though the LORD had directed Israel to go up, with Judah first. After weeping, fasting and offering sacrifices at Bethel, Israel is told by the LORD that he will deliver Benjamin into their hand, and on the third day Israel uses ambushers and a feigned retreat. The ambushers burn Gibeah, the smoke signal turns the battle, and Benjamin loses twenty-five thousand men, with only six hundred escaping to the rock of Rimmon while Israel destroys the cities of Benjamin.

l: Israel, The Book of Judges, Chapter 20
s: The children of Israel assemble as one man at Mizpah, hear the Levite's account, and vow not to go home until they have dealt with Gibeah. After Benjamin refuses to surrender the guilty men, they lose twenty-two thousand and then eighteen thousand in battle, inquire of the LORD at Bethel with weeping, fasting and offerings, and on the third day use an ambush and a feigned retreat to defeat Benjamin and burn its cities.

l: Benjamin, The Book of Judges, Chapter 20
s: Benjamin refuses to heed the other tribes' demand to deliver up the wicked men of Gibeah and gathers twenty-six thousand swordsmen, including seven hundred left-handed chosen men. It wins the first two days but is struck down on the third, losing twenty-five thousand men, with only six hundred surviving at the rock of Rimmon, and its cities, people and livestock are put to the sword and burned.

l: Gibeah, The Book of Judges, Chapter 20
s: Gibeah, a city of Benjamin, is the place where the Levite was attacked and is the target of Israel's assembly and assault. Its seven hundred chosen men fight with Benjamin, and on the third day the ambushers rush the city, strike it with the sword and set it on fire, so that the whole city goes up in smoke.

l: men of Gibeah (wicked fellows), The Book of Judges, Chapter 20
s: According to the Levite, the men of Gibeah surrounded the house by night, intended to kill him and raped his concubine until she was dead. Israel demands that the wicked men among them be delivered up for death, and Gibeah contributes seven hundred chosen men to Benjamin's army before the city is destroyed.

l: Levite (the concubine's husband), The Book of Judges, Chapter 20
s: The Levite, husband of the murdered woman, tells the assembly at Mizpah that he came to Gibeah with his concubine to spend the night and was attacked there. He says he cut her in pieces and sent them throughout Israel, and asks the people for their advice and counsel.

l: concubine (the Levite's concubine), The Book of Judges, Chapter 20
s: She is described by the Levite as having been raped by the men of Gibeah, and she is dead. Her body was cut in pieces and sent throughout the country of Israel's inheritance, which prompts the gathering of the tribes.

l: LORD, The Book of Judges, Chapter 20
s: The LORD answers Israel's inquiries at Bethel, naming Judah to go up first and later telling Israel to go up against Benjamin even after losses. On the third day he promises to deliver Benjamin into Israel's hand, and the text says the LORD struck Benjamin before Israel.

l: ambushers, The Book of Judges, Chapter 20
s: Israel sets ambushers around Gibeah, and they break out of their place when Israel's main force feigns flight at Baal Tamar. They rush Gibeah, strike the city with the sword and raise the great cloud of smoke as the appointed sign, which turns the battle against Benjamin.

l: battle between Israel and Benjamin, The Book of Judges, Chapter 20
s: Benjamin wins the first two days, killing twenty-two thousand and then eighteen thousand Israelites, using its seven hundred left-handed slingers among others. On the third day Israel draws Benjamin from the city, the ambushers burn Gibeah, and Benjamin's army is routed, with twenty-five thousand swordsmen dead and six hundred fleeing to the rock of Rimmon, where they stay four months.

l: outrage at Gibeah, The Book of Judges, Chapter 20
s: The outrage is the attack on the Levite and the rape and death of his concubine, called wickedness, lewdness and folly in Israel. It is the cause of Israel's assembly, its demand that the guilty men be put to death to put away evil from Israel, and the war that follows when Benjamin refuses.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 21
s: The men of Israel, who had sworn at Mizpah not to give their daughters to Benjamin, gather at Bethel and weep that one tribe is missing from Israel. Finding that no one from Jabesh Gilead came to the assembly, they send twelve thousand valiant men to strike its inhabitants, sparing four hundred young virgins who are brought to the camp at Shiloh. These women are given to the returned Benjamites, but there are not enough. The elders then tell the Benjamites to hide in the vineyards at the yearly feast of the LORD in Shiloh and seize wives from the dancing daughters of Shiloh, and the Benjamites do so and return to rebuild their cities. The book closes with the people going home and the remark that there was no king in Israel and everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

l: Benjamin, The Book of Judges, Chapter 21
s: Benjamin is the tribe cut off from Israel by the oath, and the people grieve for it. Its remaining men are offered peace at the rock of Rimmon, receive the 400 women of Jabesh Gilead (not enough), then seize wives from the dancing daughters of Shiloh, return to their inheritance, rebuild their cities and live in them.

l: Israel, The Book of Judges, Chapter 21
s: The children of Israel weep at Bethel, build an altar, and offer burnt and peace offerings, grieving that a tribe is lacking. They devise ways to supply Benjamin with wives without breaking their oath, and at the end each man departs to his own tribe, family and inheritance.

l: Jabesh Gilead, The Book of Judges, Chapter 21
s: Jabesh Gilead is found to be the one place that sent no one to the assembly at Mizpah. Its inhabitants are targeted by the congregation's army, and only four hundred young virgins are spared.

l: four hundred young virgins of Jabesh Gilead, The Book of Judges, Chapter 21
s: Four hundred young virgins who had not lain with a man are found among the inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead and brought to the camp at Shiloh. They are given to Benjamin, but the number is not enough for all the men.

l: LORD, The Book of Judges, Chapter 21
s: The LORD is the one before whom Israel weeps and offers sacrifices and by whom the oath was sworn. The people say he made a breach in the tribes of Israel, and his yearly feast at Shiloh provides the occasion for the seizure of wives.

l: Shiloh, The Book of Judges, Chapter 21
s: Shiloh, in the land of Canaan, is where the 400 virgins are brought to the camp. It is also the site of the yearly feast of the LORD, located north of Bethel, east of the highway from Bethel to Shechem and south of Lebonah, where the Benjamites carry off wives.

l: daughters of Shiloh, The Book of Judges, Chapter 21
s: The daughters of Shiloh come out to dance at the feast. The Benjamites, hiding in the vineyards, each catch one of them as a wife and carry them off to the land of Benjamin.

l: oath at Mizpah, The Book of Judges, Chapter 21
s: The men of Israel had sworn at Mizpah not to give their daughters to Benjamin as wives, and a curse was placed on anyone who does. A great oath also called for the death of anyone who did not come up to the LORD at Mizpah. These oaths create the problem of providing wives for Benjamin and drive the actions against Jabesh Gilead and Shiloh.

l: feast of the LORD, The Book of Judges, Chapter 21
s: The feast of the LORD is held from year to year in Shiloh. The elders choose it as the time when the Benjamites may take wives from the dancing daughters of Shiloh.

l: abduction of the daughters of Shiloh, The Book of Judges, Chapter 21
s: On the elders' instruction, the Benjamites lie in wait in the vineyards and each catch a wife from the dancing daughters of Shiloh. The elders plan to tell complaining fathers and brothers that the men took them neither in battle nor by being given, so Israel would not be guilty by giving.

l: slaughter of Jabesh Gilead, The Book of Judges, Chapter 21
s: The congregation sends twelve thousand valiant men to strike Jabesh Gilead with the sword, including women and little ones. They are told to destroy every male and every woman who has lain with a man, and the young virgins are spared.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, 1 Samuel / Chapter 1
s: Elkanah of Ramathaim Zophim, an Ephraimite, had two wives: Peninnah, who had children, and Hannah, who had none because the LORD had shut up her womb. At Shiloh, Peninnah provoked Hannah year after year, and Hannah wept in bitterness and prayed, vowing that if given a boy she would give him to the LORD all his life. Eli the priest mistook her silent prayer for drunkenness, then, learning of her sorrow, blessed her and prayed that God would grant her petition. Hannah conceived and bore Samuel, and after weaning him she brought him to the LORD's house in Shiloh with offerings and presented him to Eli, giving him to the LORD as she had vowed.

l: Elkanah, The First Book of Samuel, 1 Samuel / Chapter 1
s: Elkanah, an Ephraimite of Ramathaim Zophim, had two wives, Hannah and Peninnah, and went up yearly to worship and sacrifice at Shiloh. He gave Hannah a double portion because he loved her and asked whether he was not better to her than ten sons. He let Hannah wait until Samuel was weaned before going up, and then went with his house to offer the yearly sacrifice and his vow.

l: Hannah, The First Book of Samuel, 1 Samuel / Chapter 1
s: Hannah, Elkanah's beloved wife, was childless and was provoked yearly by Peninnah, so she wept and would not eat. At Shiloh she prayed in bitterness of soul and vowed to give a boy to the LORD all his days with no razor on his head. After Eli blessed her she ate and was no longer sad, bore Samuel, weaned him, and brought him to Eli at Shiloh to fulfill her vow.

l: Peninnah, The First Book of Samuel, 1 Samuel / Chapter 1
s: Peninnah was Elkanah's other wife and had sons and daughters, to whom Elkanah gave portions at the sacrifice. As Hannah's rival, she severely provoked Hannah year by year when they went up to the LORD's house, to irritate her.

l: Eli, The First Book of Samuel, 1 Samuel / Chapter 1
s: Eli the priest sat by the doorpost of the LORD's temple and saw Hannah's moving lips, thinking she was drunk and telling her to get rid of her wine. After she explained her sorrow, he told her to go in peace and asked that the God of Israel grant her petition. Hannah later brought the child Samuel to him.

l: Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, 1 Samuel / Chapter 1
s: Samuel was born to Hannah after the LORD remembered her, and she named him because she had asked him of the LORD. After he was weaned, he was brought young to the LORD's house in Shiloh and given to the LORD for as long as he lives.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, 1 Samuel / Chapter 1
s: The LORD of Armies is worshiped and sacrificed to at Shiloh, and is said to have shut up Hannah's womb. He is addressed in Hannah's vow, remembers her after Elkanah knew her, and gives her the petition she asked for in a son.

l: Shiloh, The First Book of Samuel, 1 Samuel / Chapter 1
s: Shiloh is the place where Elkanah went up yearly to worship and sacrifice to the LORD of Armies, and where Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas served as priests. Hannah prayed there at the LORD's house and temple, and later brought Samuel there with three bulls, an ephah of meal, and wine.

l: Hannah's vow, The First Book of Samuel, 1 Samuel / Chapter 1
s: Hannah vowed that if the LORD would look on her affliction and give her a boy, she would give him to the LORD all his life and no razor would touch his head. After Samuel's birth and weaning she fulfilled it by bringing him to Eli and declaring that she had given him to the LORD.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: Hannah prays a song of praise exalting the LORD as holy, a reverser of fortunes who raises the poor and brings down the mighty, and who will strengthen his anointed king. Elkanah returns to Ramah while the child Samuel serves the LORD before Eli the priest. Eli's sons are wicked men who despise the LORD's offering by seizing meat by force and sleeping with the women who serve at the Tent of Meeting, and Eli's rebuke goes unheeded because the LORD intends to kill them. A man of God tells Eli that the LORD will cut off his house, that Hophni and Phinehas will die in one day, and that a faithful priest will be raised up in their place. Meanwhile Samuel grows in favor with the LORD and with men, and Hannah, visited by the LORD, bears three more sons and two daughters.

l: Hannah, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: Hannah prays a song of rejoicing in the LORD's salvation. She makes her son Samuel a little robe each year and brings it when she goes up with her husband to the yearly sacrifice. The LORD visits her, and she conceives and bears three sons and two daughters.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: The LORD is praised in Hannah's song as holy, all-knowing, and the one who kills and makes alive, makes poor and rich, and raises the needy. He judges Eli's house through a man of God, declaring that he will honor those who honor him and curse those who despise him, and intends to kill Eli's sons. He promises to raise up a faithful priest with a sure house and visits Hannah with children.

l: Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: Samuel, still a child, serves the LORD before Eli the priest, clothed in a linen ephod. His mother brings him a little robe every year. He grows and increases in favor with both the LORD and men.

l: Eli, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: Eli, the priest, is very old and hears of his sons' misdeeds. He rebukes them, asking who will intercede for a man who sins against the LORD, but they do not listen. He blesses Elkanah and Hannah, then receives a message from a man of God that his house will be cut off and his two sons will die in one day.

l: sons of Eli, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: Eli's sons are called wicked men who did not know the LORD. Their servants take raw meat from worshipers by force, and they sleep with the women serving at the door of the Tent of Meeting, so their sin is very great before the LORD. They ignore their father's rebuke because the LORD intends to kill them, and the sign given is that Hophni and Phinehas will both die in one day.

l: sacrifice offerings (priests' custom), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: The priests' custom was for a servant to stab a three-toothed fork into the pot and take whatever it brought up for the priest. The servant also demanded raw meat before the fat was burned, taking it by force if refused. This led the men to despise the LORD's offering.

l: house of your father, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: The man of God recalls that the LORD revealed himself to this house in Egypt, chose it from all the tribes to be his priests, and gave it the offerings made by fire. Although the LORD had said it would walk before him forever, he now announces it will be cut off, with no old man in it, and its survivors will beg for priestly positions for bread.

l: man of God, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: The man of God comes to Eli with the LORD's message of judgment. He recounts the house's privileges, accuses Eli of honoring his sons above the LORD, and announces the end of the house, the sign of the deaths of Hophni and Phinehas, and a coming faithful priest.

l: Hannah's song, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: Hannah's song exalts the LORD as holy, a rock, and a God of knowledge who weighs actions. It describes reversals in which the mighty are broken, the hungry are satisfied, the barren bears seven, and the poor are lifted from the dust. It ends by declaring that the LORD will judge the ends of the earth and strengthen his king and anointed.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 3
s: The child Samuel serves the LORD under Eli, whose eyesight is failing, at a time when the LORD's word is rare. The LORD calls Samuel three times, and each time Samuel runs to Eli, who finally perceives that the LORD is calling and tells Samuel to answer, 'Speak, LORD; for your servant hears.' The LORD then tells Samuel he will judge Eli's house forever because Eli did not restrain his sons, who brought a curse on themselves. Samuel, afraid, finally tells Eli everything when pressed, and Eli responds, 'It is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him.' Samuel grows, the LORD is with him, and all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knows he is established as a prophet.

l: Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 3
s: Samuel, a child ministering to the LORD before Eli, hears the LORD call him three times and mistakes the voice for Eli's until Eli instructs him how to answer. He then receives the LORD's message of judgment against Eli's house, fears to tell Eli, but reports it all when Eli presses him. He grows, none of his words fall to the ground, and all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knows he is established as the LORD's prophet.

l: Eli, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 3
s: Eli, whose eyes have grown dim, is woken three times by Samuel and realizes the third time that the LORD is calling the child. He tells Samuel to answer 'Speak, LORD; for your servant hears.' After Samuel reports the judgment against his house, Eli accepts it, saying 'It is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him.'

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 3
s: The LORD calls Samuel repeatedly, then comes and stands and speaks, announcing a coming act in Israel and judgment on Eli's house. He is with Samuel as he grows, lets none of his words fall to the ground, and appears again in Shiloh, revealing himself to Samuel by his word.

l: house of Eli, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 3
s: The LORD declares he will perform against Eli's house all he has spoken, from beginning to end, and will judge it forever. The cause given is the iniquity Eli knew of: his sons brought a curse on themselves and he did not restrain them. The LORD has sworn that the iniquity will not be removed by sacrifice or offering forever.

l: vision, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 3
s: The vision is the LORD's message to Samuel of judgment on Eli's house, at a time when visions were not many. Samuel is afraid to show it to Eli, but tells him every bit when Eli demands it under an oath-like charge.

l: LORD's call to Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 3
s: The LORD calls Samuel three times, and each time Samuel goes to Eli, thinking Eli called, because Samuel does not yet know the LORD and the LORD's word has not yet been revealed to him. After Eli's instruction, the LORD calls a fourth time, 'Samuel! Samuel!', and Samuel answers, 'Speak; for your servant hears.'

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: Israel fights the Philistines at Ebenezer and Aphek and loses about four thousand men. The elders bring the ark of the LORD's covenant from Shiloh, along with Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas, and Israel shouts in celebration. The frightened Philistines nonetheless fight, defeat Israel again with thirty thousand footmen dead, capture the ark, and kill Hophni and Phinehas. A man of Benjamin runs to Shiloh with the news, and Eli, ninety-eight years old, falls from his seat and dies after hearing of the ark's capture. Phinehas' wife, hearing of the ark, her father-in-law and her husband, gives birth and names her son Ichabod, saying the glory has departed from Israel.

l: Israel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: Israel was defeated by the Philistines, losing about four thousand men, then brought the ark into camp and shouted greatly. In the second battle Israel was defeated again, thirty thousand footmen fell, and each man fled to his tent.

l: Philistines, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: The Philistines defeated Israel at the first battle, killing about four thousand men. They feared the ark and the 'mighty gods' who struck the Egyptians, urged each other to fight like men, then defeated Israel again, killed thirty thousand footmen, and captured the ark.

l: Ark of the covenant, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: The elders had the ark brought from Shiloh to the camp so it might save Israel, and Israel shouted when it arrived. The Philistines feared it, but in the second battle it was taken.

l: Eli, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: Eli was ninety-eight years old and blind, sitting by the road watching because his heart trembled for the ark. When the man told him that his sons were dead and the ark captured, he fell backward from his seat, broke his neck and died, having judged Israel forty years.

l: Hophni, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: Hophni, a son of Eli, was with the ark when it was brought to the camp. He was slain in the battle.

l: Phinehas, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: Phinehas, a son of Eli, was with the ark when it was brought to the camp. He was slain in the battle, leaving a wife who was with child.

l: Phinehas' wife, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: Phinehas' wife, near to giving birth, heard that the ark was taken and that her father-in-law and husband were dead. She bowed down and gave birth to a son, did not answer the women who comforted her, and died, naming the child Ichabod.

l: Ichabod, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: Ichabod was born to Phinehas' wife as she was dying after the news of the ark's capture. His mother named him Ichabod, saying 'The glory has departed from Israel.'

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: The elders asked why the LORD had defeated Israel before the Philistines, and sought to bring the LORD's ark, the ark of the covenant of the LORD of Armies who sits above the cherubim. The Philistines recalled that these gods struck the Egyptians with plagues.

l: man of Benjamin, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: A man of Benjamin ran out of the army to Shiloh the same day, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. He told the city and then Eli that Israel had fled, Eli's sons were dead and the ark was captured.

l: Shiloh, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: The ark was brought out of Shiloh to the army's camp. The man of Benjamin brought news of the defeat there, and all the city cried out; Eli died at its gate.

l: battle between Israel and the Philistines, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: Israel encamped beside Ebenezer and the Philistines at Aphek; in the first fight Israel lost about four thousand men. After the ark was brought, a second battle ended in a great slaughter of thirty thousand Israelite footmen, the ark's capture and the deaths of Hophni and Phinehas.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: The Philistines bring God's ark from Ebenezer to Ashdod and place it in the house of Dagon beside Dagon. Two mornings in a row Dagon is found fallen on his face before the ark, and the second time his head and palms are cut off on the threshold, leaving only the torso. The LORD's hand is heavy on Ashdod, striking its people with tumors, so the men of Ashdod gather the Philistine lords and send the ark to Gath. The same affliction strikes Gath, and the ark is then sent to Ekron, where the Ekronites cry out in fear and demand that it be sent back to its own place. Deadly panic and tumors afflict Ekron, and the cry of the city goes up to heaven.

l: Ark of the covenant, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
