s: The ark is taken by the Philistines from Ebenezer to Ashdod and set in Dagon's house beside Dagon. It is then moved to Gath and Ekron, and the people of each place are struck as it arrives. The lords of the Philistines finally say it should be sent away to its own place.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: The LORD's ark is found with Dagon fallen on his face before it, and his hand is heavy on Ashdod, Gath and Ekron. He strikes the people with tumors and causes great confusion and deadly panic. The Ashdodites say his hand is severe on them and on Dagon.

l: Dagon, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: Dagon is found fallen on his face before the ark two mornings in a row; the first time he is set back in his place. The second time his head and both palms are cut off on the threshold, leaving only his torso. Because of this, neither his priests nor those entering his house step on the threshold in Ashdod to this day.

l: Philistines, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: The Philistines take the ark to Ashdod and place it in Dagon's house. Their lords are gathered twice to decide what to do with it, and they send it first to Gath and then to Ekron. In the end they say to send it away to its own place so it will not kill them.

l: Ashdod, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: Ashdod is where the ark is first brought, and where Dagon falls and is broken before it. The LORD's hand is heavy on the city and its borders, which are struck with tumors.

l: people of Ashdod, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: The people of Ashdod rise early to find Dagon fallen, and set him up again before finding him broken. They are struck with tumors, and the men conclude the ark of the God of Israel cannot stay with them. They gather the Philistine lords and have the ark carried to Gath.

l: Gath, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: Gath receives the ark after Ashdod. The LORD's hand is against the city with a very great confusion, and men both small and great are struck so that tumors break out on them.

l: Ekron, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: Ekron receives the ark after it is sent from Gath. The city falls into deadly panic, the hand of God is very heavy there, and those who do not die are struck with tumors. The cry of the city goes up to heaven.

l: Ekronites, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: As the ark arrives, the Ekronites cry out that it has been brought to kill them and their people. They gather the Philistine lords and urge that the ark be sent away to its own place so it will not kill them.

l: tumors, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: Tumors are the affliction the LORD sends on Ashdod and its borders, then on the men of Gath, small and great. At Ekron, those who did not die were struck with them.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: After the LORD's ark has been in Philistine territory seven months, the Philistines ask their priests and diviners how to send it back, and are told to return it with a trespass offering of five golden tumors and five golden mice, citing the Egyptians and Pharaoh as a warning against hardening their hearts. They put the ark and the offering on a new cart pulled by two milk cows never yoked, as a test of whether the LORD's hand struck them. The cows go straight to Beth Shemesh, where the people reaping wheat rejoice, split the cart's wood, and offer the cows as a burnt offering while the Levites set the ark on a great stone. The LORD strikes down fifty thousand seventy men of Beth Shemesh for looking into the ark, and the survivors, mourning, ask who can stand before this holy God and send messengers to Kiriath Jearim to come take the ark.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: The LORD's hand is understood by the Philistines to have struck them, and the priests advise honoring him with a trespass offering. He receives burnt offerings at Beth Shemesh, then strikes fifty thousand seventy of its men because they looked into his ark. The survivors call him a holy God before whom no one can stand.

l: Ark of the covenant, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: The ark stays seven months in Philistine country, then is sent back on a new cart with a box of golden jewels beside it. It arrives at Beth Shemesh, where Levites set it and the box on the great stone. Because men looked into it, many die, and the people send word to Kiriath Jearim to come bring it up.

l: Philistines, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: The Philistines consult priests and diviners about returning the ark and agree to send a trespass offering of five golden tumors and five golden mice, one for each lord. They test whether the LORD's hand struck them by seeing if the cows go to Beth Shemesh. Their five lords follow the cart to the border and return to Ekron the same day.

l: trespass offering, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: The offering is prescribed as five golden tumors and five golden mice, matching the number of the Philistine lords, as images of the tumors and the mice that mar the land. It is placed in a box beside the ark on the cart. The tumors are listed as one each for Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron, and the mice match all the cities of the five lords.

l: new cart, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: The new cart is prepared by the Philistines to carry the ark, with the box of golden jewels at its side. It is drawn by two cows to the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh and stops by a great stone. Its wood is then split for the burnt offering.

l: milk cows, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: Two milk cows that have never borne a yoke are tied to the cart while their calves are shut up at home. They go straight along the highway to Beth Shemesh, lowing and not turning aside. The people of Beth Shemesh then offer them as a burnt offering to the LORD.

l: Beth Shemesh, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: Beth Shemesh is the border town the cows head for, which the Philistines take as a sign that the LORD struck them. The ark comes to the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh, where a great stone remains to this day. The town suffers a great slaughter and then sends messengers to Kiriath Jearim.

l: people of Beth Shemesh, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: The people are reaping wheat in the valley when they see the ark and rejoice. They offer the cows as a burnt offering and make further sacrifices the same day. After the slaughter they mourn, ask who can stand before the holy God, and send messengers asking Kiriath Jearim to take the ark.

l: slaughter of Beth Shemesh men, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: The LORD strikes fifty thousand seventy of the men of Beth Shemesh because they looked into the ark. The people mourn this great slaughter. It leads them to ask who can stand before the holy God and to send the ark away to Kiriath Jearim.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 7
s: After the men of Kiriath Jearim bring the LORD's ark into Abinadab's house and consecrate Eleazar to keep it, Israel laments for twenty years. Samuel calls Israel to return to the LORD with all their hearts and put away foreign gods, and the people remove the Baals and Ashtaroth and serve the LORD only. At Mizpah, Israel fasts, confesses sin, and Samuel judges them and prays for them; when the Philistines advance, Samuel offers a lamb as a burnt offering and the LORD thunders and confuses the Philistines, who are struck down and pursued by Israel. Samuel sets up a stone called Ebenezer, the Philistines are subdued, Israel's cities and border are restored, and Samuel judges Israel all his life, circuiting Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah and returning to Ramah, where he builds an altar.

l: Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 7
s: Samuel exhorts Israel to put away foreign gods and serve the LORD only, gathers them at Mizpah, prays for them, and judges them there. He offers a suckling lamb as a burnt offering and cries to the LORD, who answers him, then sets up the Ebenezer stone. He judges Israel all his life, circuiting Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, and returns to Ramah, where he builds an altar to the LORD.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 7
s: The LORD's ark is brought into Abinadab's house at Kiriath Jearim, and Israel laments after him for twenty years. He answers Samuel's cry, thunders on the Philistines and confuses them so they are struck down before Israel. His hand is against the Philistines all the days of Samuel, and Samuel says he has helped Israel until now.

l: Israel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 7
s: Israel laments after the LORD for twenty years, then removes the Baals and Ashtaroth and serves the LORD only. At Mizpah they fast, pour out water, and confess they have sinned, and they ask Samuel not to stop crying to the LORD for them. They pursue and strike the Philistines, recover their cities and border from Ekron to Gath, and have peace with the Amorites.

l: Philistines, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 7
s: The lords of the Philistines go up against Israel when they hear Israel has gathered at Mizpah. The LORD thunders and confuses them, and they are struck down and pursued to Beth Kar. They are subdued, stop coming within Israel's border, and the cities they took from Israel are restored, from Ekron to Gath.

l: Mizpah, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 7
s: Mizpah is where Israel gathers to fast, pour out water before the LORD, and confess their sin, and where Samuel judges them. Israel's men go out from Mizpah to pursue the Philistines, and Samuel sets the Ebenezer stone between Mizpah and Shen. It is one of the places on Samuel's yearly judging circuit.

l: battle at Mizpah, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 7
s: When the Philistines come near to fight Israel while Samuel is offering the burnt offering, the LORD thunders on them and confuses them, and they are struck down before Israel. Israel's men pursue them from Mizpah to under Beth Kar. Samuel marks the victory with a stone named Ebenezer, and the Philistines are subdued afterward.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 8
s: In old age, Samuel appoints his sons Joel and Abijah as judges in Beersheba, but they take bribes and pervert justice. The elders of Israel come to Samuel at Ramah and demand a king to judge them like all the nations. Displeased, Samuel prays, and the LORD tells him to heed the people because they have rejected the LORD as their king, while also warning them solemnly. Samuel describes how a king will take their sons, daughters, fields, produce, servants, and flocks, and warn that the LORD will not answer their cry; the people refuse to listen and insist on a king, so the LORD tells Samuel to give them one and Samuel sends the men home.

l: Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 8
s: Samuel, now old, made his sons judges over Israel. He was displeased by the elders' request for a king and prayed to the LORD, then relayed the LORD's words and a warning about the king's ways to the people. When they refused to listen, he repeated their words to the LORD, was told to make them a king, and sent the men of Israel home.

l: sons (Samuel's sons), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 8
s: Joel, the firstborn, and Abijah, the second son, were made judges in Beersheba. They did not walk in their father's ways, but pursued dishonest gain, took bribes, and perverted justice.

l: Israel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 8
s: Israel is the nation Samuel's sons judged and whose elders and people demand a king to be like all the nations. The LORD notes its history of forsaking him and serving other gods since he brought it out of Egypt. At the end the men of Israel are told to go each to their own city.

l: elders of Israel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 8
s: The elders gathered and came to Samuel at Ramah. They cited his age and his sons' conduct as reasons and asked him to make them a king to judge them like all the nations.

l: people (Israel), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 8
s: The people were told the LORD's words and the way of the king, but refused to listen to Samuel. They insisted on having a king so they would be like all the nations, with a king who would judge them, go out before them, and fight their battles.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 8
s: The LORD told Samuel to listen to the people, saying they had rejected him as their king, consistent with their forsaking him since the exodus from Egypt. He directed Samuel to warn them solemnly and show them the way of the king, and finally to heed their voice and make them a king. Samuel warned that the LORD will not answer them when they cry out because of their king.

l: king (requested by Israel), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 8
s: The people want a king to judge them, go before them, and fight their battles like the nations' kings. The LORD, after Samuel's warning and the people's refusal, tells Samuel to make them a king. No king is named in this unit.

l: the way of the king, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 8
s: Samuel describes it as the king taking sons for chariots, horsemen, captains, plowing, reaping, and making weapons, and daughters as perfumers, cooks, and bakers. He will also take the best fields, vineyards, and olive groves, a tenth of seed, vineyards, and flocks, and servants, young men, and donkeys. The people will become his servants and will cry out in vain to the LORD.

l: request for a king, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 8
s: The elders made the request at Ramah, citing Samuel's age and his sons' conduct. It displeased Samuel, and the LORD said it was a rejection of himself as king. Despite the warnings, the people persisted, and the LORD told Samuel to grant it.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: Saul, the tall and handsome son of Kish, a Benjamite, is sent by his father with a servant to look for lost donkeys. After searching the hill country of Ephraim and the lands of Shalishah, Shaalim, and Benjamin without success, they reach the land of Zuph, where the servant suggests consulting the man of God in the city. The LORD had told Samuel the day before that he would send a man of Benjamin to be anointed prince over Israel to save it from the Philistines, and he identifies Saul when he appears. Samuel tells Saul the donkeys are found, hints that Israel desires him, and seats him in the place of honor at a sacrifice feast with about thirty guests, giving him the reserved portion. The next morning Samuel sends the servant ahead so that he can tell Saul God's message alone.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: Saul, a tall and handsome Benjamite and son of Kish, is sent to find his father's lost donkeys and, after a fruitless search, agrees to consult the seer on his servant's advice. Samuel, informed by the LORD, tells him the donkeys are found and that Israel's desire is for him, though Saul protests that he is of the smallest tribe and least family. He is honored at the feast with the reserved portion and, at the end, is told to stand still to hear God's message.

l: Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: Samuel, the seer, was told by the LORD a day earlier that a man of Benjamin would come to be anointed prince over Israel, and he recognizes Saul when he sees him. He invites Saul to eat with him at the high place, tells him the donkeys are found, seats him in the best place, and has the reserved portion set before him. The next morning he sends Saul's servant ahead so he can give Saul God's message.

l: Kish, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: Kish, a mighty man of valor of Benjamin, is the son of Abiel and father of Saul. When his donkeys are lost, he sends Saul and a servant to look for them.

l: servant (Saul's servant), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: The servant accompanies Saul in the search and, at Zuph, proposes consulting the honored man of God in the city. He offers the fourth part of a shekel of silver as a gift when Saul worries they have nothing to bring. At the end Samuel has him go on ahead of Saul and Samuel.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: The LORD revealed to Samuel a day beforehand that he would send a Benjamite to be anointed prince over his people, to save them from the Philistines because he had looked on their cry. When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD identified him as the man who would have authority over his people.

l: donkeys (Kish's donkeys), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: Kish's donkeys were lost, which prompted Saul's journey through Ephraim, Shalishah, Shaalim, and Benjamin, where they were not found. Samuel later tells Saul they were lost three days earlier and have been found.

l: Israel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: Israel is the people the LORD says he has looked upon because their cry has come to him, and whom the chosen man is to save from the Philistines. Samuel says all Israel desires Saul and his father's house. The text notes that no one among the children of Israel was more handsome than Saul.

l: city (where Samuel lives), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: Saul and his servant go up to this city, where young maidens drawing water tell them the seer has just arrived for the people's sacrifice. Samuel meets them within it, and Saul talks with him on the housetop that night. They walk to the end of the city the next morning, where Samuel sends the servant ahead.

l: high place, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: The high place is where the people hold a sacrifice that day and where Samuel goes up to bless it before the invited guests eat. Samuel tells Saul to go up there ahead of him to eat. Afterward they come down from it into the city.

l: sacrifice feast, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: The people hold a sacrifice at the high place, and they will not eat until Samuel arrives to bless it. Saul and his servant are seated in the best place among about thirty invited guests. Saul is served the reserved thigh that Samuel had told the cook to set aside for him.
